channel.title: Noticias del Mundo — Ciencia
channel.description: Noticias de ciencia de todas las fuentes configuradas.

item.title: AI virtual cell technology could reveal how genetic changes and drugs alter cells
item.description: Today's artificial intelligence models can predict whether someone with a genetic change will develop a disease, but cannot answer two critical questions: Why did the disease occur, and how do we design a treatment? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Building structured-light systems in three dimensions
item.description: Structured light has become an important tool across modern optics. By shaping properties such as amplitude, phase, polarization and spatial mode, researchers can create light fields with capabilities beyond those of conventional laser beams. These engineered light fields are finding applications in communications, imaging, sensing, optical computing and quantum photonics. However, many structured-light systems still rely on multiple discrete optical components that require careful alignment and occupy significant space. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Innovative technology offers a bold new vision for monitoring ocean health
item.description: On an early October morning, as MBARI's research vessel Paragon left Moss Landing with three robots loaded on its deck, Monterey Bay was showing off. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New mondo grass species found in Yunnan
item.description: Botanists have described a new Ophiopogon species from the Yunnan Wenshan National Nature Reserve in southeastern China. They named it Ophiopogon longiscapus for its unusually long flowering stalk, or scape. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Organizational science offers new lens for studying extremism
item.description: Accepting the Republican nomination for president in 1964, Barry Goldwater declared, "I would remind you that extremism in the defense of liberty is no vice!" His statement illustrates how the cause being defended can shape judgments about the actions taken in its name. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New study: The last bird to go extinct in NZ has lessons for saving other species
item.description: The last bird to go extinct in Aotearoa New Zealand was a tiny wren that disappeared from a small island off the southern tip of Rakiura Stewart Island around 1972. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NEPTUNE poised to replace Navy's global weather model, improving forecasts over open ocean
item.description: The U.S. Naval Research Laboratory-developed Navy Environmental Prediction sysTem Utilizing a Nonhydrostatic Engine, known as NEPTUNE, is poised to become an operational Navy weather prediction capability, providing improved environmental forecasts to support naval operations around the globe. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI companions could help reduce loneliness, study finds
item.description: AI companions could help reduce loneliness by creating a greater sense of belonging and improving self-esteem, according to new research from Durham University Business School. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Q&A: Making hydrogen peroxide without using precious metals
item.description: Hydrogen peroxide is used in many industrial processes, with several million tons of it being manufactured worldwide every year. Whereas the standard production method requires rare precious metals, chemists from Rutgers University–Newark in the US and the University of Bonn have now described an alternative technique that does away with these metals, making it potentially cheaper and more sustainable. Their findings have now been published in the journal Nature Communications. In the following interview, the authors describe the technology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle
item.description: Researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a compound that could transform weight-loss treatment by helping the body burn more energy instead of suppressing appetite like Ozempic and Wegovy. In mice, the compound boosted energy expenditure by up to 18%, improved blood sugar control, reduced liver fat, and promoted weight loss without significant muscle loss. Even more promising, combining it with existing GLP-1 medications produced greater benefits than either treatment alone. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Mercury-bound X-ray telescope delivers first images after eight years in space
item.description: The first data from a U.K.-built instrument heading to Mercury have provided observations of one of the brightest X-ray sources in the sky from aboard the ESA/JAXA BepiColombo spacecraft in the inner solar system. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'PAC-MAN' capsules that gobble up particles in turbulent water show promise for filtration and drug delivery
item.description: Scientists have created hollow capsules with single openings that can selectively filter particles thanks to the turbulence in surrounding waters—at times, ingesting particles like PAC-MAN eating up dots. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Britain should treat healthy seas as essential infrastructure, say scientists
item.description: Researchers are calling for lasting investment in healthy seas to support food security, protect coastlines and strengthen economic resilience. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The secret of 'strange metals' may lie in quantum statistics, not collisions
item.description: In an ordinary metal, electrons behave like well-defined particles that occasionally bump into imperfections or vibrations of the crystal. Many materials with strong electron–electron interactions, including the copper-oxide (cuprate) superconductors, break these rules. In these "strange metals," electrical resistance rises in a straight line with temperature over a very wide range. Electrons seem to lose their momentum at the fastest rate quantum mechanics allows, the so-called Planckian limit. What causes this is still an open question. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Euclid's hunt for strong gravitational lenses is off to a strong start
item.description: If dark matter and dark energy were a part of our everyday lives, we would live in a perpetual state of dumbfoundedness. Imagine living in a world where 95% of the matter and energy were invisible and undetectable. It would be impossible to make sense of our surroundings. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Staying alive in marsh muck: The tiny 'snorkels' cattails grow manipulate soil chemistry
item.description: Cattails are a familiar sight in wetlands, where they thrive in both brackish and freshwater marshes. But surviving in waterlogged soil presents a challenge; their roots need oxygen in an environment where very little is available. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Dual-purpose polymer dots could combine bioimaging and light-triggered cell death in one material
item.description: A research team led by professor Youhei Takeda at the University of Osaka, in collaboration with professor Zachary M. Hudson at the University of British Columbia (UBC) in Canada, has developed a polymer material that combines fluorescent cell imaging with the potential to kill cancer cells when activated by light. The material could offer a simpler approach to developing "nanotheranostic" technologies, which bring disease imaging and treatment together in a single platform. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Individual meerkats are ace solo navigators
item.description: After meerkats emerge each morning from their burrow to warm in the early sun, there's one thing on their collective mind, and that's to find food. They navigate communally as they head off, working slowly along their route before returning home swiftly at the end of the day. But although the tight-knit band navigates as one, some members of the clan could be more experienced after roaming solo, shaping the community's maneuvers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How microbes make drug-like chemicals without damaging themselves
item.description: University of Michigan researchers have discovered a mechanism that enables microscopic organisms like bacteria and fungi to produce drug-like molecules—compounds that can fight infections or kill cancer cells—without damaging themselves. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: ESA's Hera probe uses 'superhuman' vision to inspect NASA's asteroid crash site
item.description: Around four years ago, humanity intentionally hit an asteroid. The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) was by pretty much all measures a resounding success when it struck the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos going more than 22,000 kilometers per hour (13,700 miles per hour). However, we still don't know just how much of a success it actually was—DART was a one-way mission with no real way to track the results of the impact close up. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: If tiny 'primordial' black holes exist, here's how we might find them
item.description: Scientists have hypothesized that, in the fraction of a second following the Big Bang, minute black holes may have been forged within tiny, dense pockets that collapsed under their own gravity. If these primordial black holes are ever found, they could represent a significant component of dark matter—the invisible substance that makes up most of the universe's matter. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Voyager 1 spacecraft reaches one light-day milestone
item.description: NASA's Voyager 1 probe, which has been traveling through space for nearly 50 years, hit a milestone distance of one light-day away from Earth on Wednesday. Already the most distant man-made object in the universe, the spacecraft is now about 26 billion kilometers (16 billion miles) away, according to the US space agency. That is the distance a particle of light can travel in 24 hours. FRANCE 24's Emerald Maxwell reports. Fuente: France 24 - English.
item.dc:creator: FRANCE24

item.title: The snake with a built-in egg peeler
item.description: Dr. Arthur Tiutenko from FAU and colleagues from LMU München and the South African National Museum in Bloemfontein discovered a new species of snake in the Harenna Forest, on the southern slopes of Ethiopia's Bale Mountains: Dasypeltis albigularis, or the white-throated egg-eater. "Three other new species in this genus are still waiting in line," the zoologist adds. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How a tiny chemical mark on a protein can be placed to double gene activity
item.description: Tiny chemical marks on histones—the proteins that package our DNA—can profoundly influence gene activity without changing the underlying DNA sequence. One such mark, known as histone acetylation, plays a crucial role in regulating gene expression and is frequently disrupted in diseases such as cancer. Researchers, however, wondered how the enzymes responsible for adding these marks know exactly where to place them. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Lonely shoppers demonstrate less compassion in their purchases than others, study shows
item.description: Chronically lonely people are less likely to buy products that benefit others, such as fair-trade or child-labor-free goods, according to a new study by researchers at Concordia and the University of the Fraser Valley. The team ran four studies involving more than 1,400 participants across North America. Each person completed a standard loneliness questionnaire, then chose between ordinary products and versions that cost 15% to 20% more but carried an ethical or environmental label. Items included toothpaste, chocolate bars, jackets and backpacks. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Light-activated nanoparticles may help treat head and neck cancer
item.description: For patients with head and neck cancer, treatment can come at a high cost to their quality of life, affecting their ability to speak, swallow and even breathe due to invasive procedures. Now, Penn State researchers have developed a light-activated nanoparticle system with the long-term goal of shrinking tumors while limiting exposure to healthy tissue and improving patients' quality of life after cancer treatment. Penn State has licensed the technology to Illuminate Therapeutics, which is advancing its preclinical development. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ethiopian volcano's mysterious methane outburst may have a culprit—magma that never erupted
item.description: Experts were puzzled when satellite observations showed a volcano in Ethiopia emitting huge quantities of methane despite not erupting, but a team of researchers led by the University of Bristol believe they have discovered why this happened—and their findings could have implications for historical climate change research. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ahead of Giving Tuesday, study finds charitable giving often misses communities with greatest need
item.description: As Giving Tuesday approaches, a recent study led by a University of Massachusetts Amherst public policy researcher finds that communities with greater economic disadvantage typically see less private charitable giving—despite having greater needs in many cases. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Remote jobs diminish hiring bias against mothers
item.description: The "motherhood penalty"—a workplace bias that assumes mothers are less committed to their careers, resulting in fewer opportunities, lower pay and slower advancement—could be reduced by shifting jobs from in-person to remote, according to new research by Claire Daviss, assistant professor of organizational behavior at the ILR School. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Optical DNA mapping assembles yeast genomes at chromosome scale
item.description: Large, complex genomes remain difficult to characterize accurately, even with modern DNA sequencing. Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology have now extended an optical genome mapping approach, previously demonstrated for bacterial genomes, to more complex eukaryotic genomes. Using two yeast species, they generated optical maps covering entire chromosomes, including large repetitive regions that are particularly difficult to reconstruct. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Improving hydrogen production from water can support abundant global crops
item.description: Water, at least in its purest form, contains hydrogen and oxygen. In 1800, scientists first used electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen gases. Today, this process, known as water electrolysis, is widely used to produce hydrogen for industrial purposes, including manufacturing ammonia for agricultural fertilizers that sustain global food production. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: X-rays reveal fleeting intermediate step as iron-containing molecule responds to light
item.description: A research team has traced how a molecule rearranges its electrons when excited by light. The findings, published in Angewandte Chemie International Edition, help clarify a long-standing question and open new possibilities for studying chemistry in motion, such as bonds breaking or forming—fundamental steps in reactions involving catalysts and biological molecules. The collaboration included Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin (HZB), the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Villigen, Switzerland, and European XFEL. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New research explains how far people will go for a day at the park
item.description: A park two miles (3.2 kilometers) from home might seem close enough for a Saturday outing. In metropolitan Detroit, though, park visits had already fallen to about half their modeled peak by that distance. In metropolitan Minneapolis, the same drop took nearly five miles (8 kilometers). And in the New York metropolitan area, with its extensive transit network, visitation fell by half at about 2.3 miles (3.7 kilometers). A park's reach, it turns out, depends a great deal on where it is. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Modified genetic method allows researchers to quantify roots growing underground
item.description: Plant scientists know that what grows above the soil doesn't offer enough information to understand an entire plant community. Different species contribute differently to belowground biomass, and those differences matter for soil health and ecosystem functioning. However, digging up roots to separate and identify them by species, especially when many plants are growing together underground, can be difficult and time-consuming, according to a team of researchers in the College of Agricultural Sciences at Penn State. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cell skeleton networks stiffen like wool when compressed, experiments reveal
item.description: As they move and push against obstacles, cells generate forces. These forces originate in their internal skeleton, some parts of which behave like wool. This mechanical property has been revealed by scientists from the CNRS, Université Paris Cité and Université Paris-Saclay. This study is published in the journal Nature. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cryptography-inspired method speeds up searches for elusive pulsars
item.description: An international team of scientists has developed a method that can find pulsars in publicly available NASA data about a million times faster than before. This opens the door to discovering many more of these rapidly spinning objects. A paper describing the results was published in Physical Review Letters. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Music industry is tone-deaf to its own gender imbalance, experiments show
item.description: Men outnumber women by four to one among performers booked at live music venues, but a new study by the University of Portsmouth has found no evidence that audiences systematically prefer male singing voices. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI helps researchers track beluga whales using aerial drone images
item.description: For Arctic researchers, counting beluga whales from the air can mean painstakingly examining thousands of aerial images—searching for animals that may be difficult to see and even harder to distinguish from one another. The challenge is especially significant when researchers are trying to identify calves, whose smaller size, lower numbers and variable appearance can make them easy to miss. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why do so many people have Neanderthal DNA?
item.description: Neanderthal DNA makes up about 2% of the genome of most non-Africans. When and how did that mixing take place, and what does it mean for modern humans? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI models favour US and UK accents, score Chinese and Nigerian ones lowest, study finds
item.description: Ask an artificial intelligence model to grade a job interview or test answers, and a person’s accent may change the score. That is according to new University of Washington research that looked at how some of the most advanced AI models rated English speakers with different accents, both on what they said and how they said it. In the scripted tests, every speaker said the same words, and AI models transcribed the accented speech accurately, meaning the models understood the accents just fine.... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Tribune News Service

item.title: The Euclid space telescope has spotted 31 ancient quasars, including two record-breakers
item.description: The Euclid space telescope has made a groundbreaking discovery by identifying 31 ancient quasars, significantly contributing to the field of astronomy. Notably, two of these quasars hold the record for their vast distances, originating when the Universe was just 670 million years old. Their light journeyed over 13 billion years to reach Earth, offering unparalleled insights into the early stages of cosmic history. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: CEOs are getting richer, even when their companies aren't
item.description: Corporate CEOs are collecting enormous paychecks, even when their companies struggle to deliver results. New research from Case Western Reserve University suggests the problem isn't just how much executives earn; it's also how they're paid. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Pathogen P. aeruginosa uses protein to limit entry of last-resort antibiotic
item.description: Bacteria have many strategies for defending themselves against antibiotics. Some destroy the drug, others pump it out or alter its target. They can also, more simply, prevent it from getting in. A team at the University of Geneva (UNIGE) has discovered how Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a bacterium responsible for infections that are often difficult to treat, very rapidly restricts the entry of imipenem, an antibiotic reserved for the most critical cases. Published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, these findings reveal a mechanism of antibiotic resistance and open up new… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Unusual magnetism revealed in a simple metal's electron spins
item.description: Magnets are usually associated with a familiar property: they produce a magnetic field because the magnetic moments of their electrons align. But nature allows much more unusual forms of magnetic order. An international research team has now identified compelling experimental evidence for p-wave magnetism in europium silicide (EuSi), a chemically simple metallic compound. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How tiger worms could help tackle the global sanitation problem
item.description: Michael Templeton is professor of public health engineering in the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering at Imperial College London and co-chair of the Imperial Global Development Lab Advisory Board. He holds the Oxfam and Water for People / Royal Academy of Engineering Research Chair in Global Sanitation Technology and is currently head of the environmental and water resource engineering section within the department. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: US and Iran once practiced diplomacy through archaeology—that legacy need not lie in ruins
item.description: When a U.S. airstrike struck Tehran's Arg Square on March 2, 2026, Golestan Palace was not the target. But it was close enough. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: More than 1,700 bee species are unique to islands, first global assessment finds
item.description: More than 1,700 bee species are found only on islands, the first global checklist of island bees shows. If you like bees and island destinations, the best places to visit are in the Mediterranean. Islands like Sicily and Cyprus are where you find the highest diversity of bee species in the world. Bee connoisseurs will also appreciate large tropical islands like Hawaii and Madagascar, where they'll find unique bee species that live only on that particular island. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Challenge: Public Input on Life and the World in 2075
item.description: NASA’s Transformational Tools and Technologies (TTT) is gathering public perspectives on life today and how the world may change by 2075. This challenge asks for conceptual ideas about life in 2075 across four challenge topics. Ideas should explore how future aviation or aerospace systems could: Ideas should be conceptual rather than technical. Award: $20,000 in […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Bailey Light

item.title: Draft of COP31 cover text drops references to fossil fuel phase-out, net zero dates
item.description: A major concern raised by developing countries, of phasing out unilateral trade measures such as the CBAM (Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism) by 2027, that was present in the earlier draft has also been eliminated Fuente: The Hindu - International.

item.title: NASA conducts latest RS-25 engine test in support of future Artemis missions
item.description: NASA tested RS-25 engine No. 10001 on Nov. 18 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi. Test teams fired the developmental engine for the planned duration of three minutes and 20 seconds (200 seconds). While this developmental engine will not be used in flight, the hot […] Publicado también por: NASA. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA's Voyager 1 phones home from record one light-day away, 49 years after launch
item.description: Nasa’s Voyager 1 has phoned home from one light-day away, humanity’s first emissary to cross this monumental threshold way out in interstellar space. Flight controllers received the spacecraft’s call on Thursday, exactly 24 hours after it was sent. That is how long it took for the radio signal to traverse the more than 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometres) at the speed of light. “Travelling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveller,”... Publicado también por: South China Morning Post. Fuente: France 24 - English.
item.dc:creator: FRANCE 24

item.title: This year's humpback whale migration was missing something vital—the calves and their mothers
item.description: After centuries of whaling, humpback whales of the Southern Hemisphere were close to extinction. As few as 5,000 animals were left in the oceans. But after efforts to end whaling culminated in a 1985 moratorium, the whales began one of the biggest comebacks in conservation. Around 50,000 humpback whales now migrate along the eastern Australian coastline. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Data centers damage air quality long-distance, study reveals
item.description: The rapid expansion of data centers for artificial intelligence causes negative health and air quality impacts in regions far from where the brick-and-mortar facilities are located, according to a new study by MIT researchers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Spirituality and religiosity associated with better quality of life in older adults
item.description: Researchers Alessandra Buja and Sohail Akhtar at the University of Padova in Italy conducted a meta-analysis of studies looking at aging adults' quality of life in relation to spirituality and religiosity. Their findings, published Nov. 19 in the open-access journal PLOS Aging and Health, suggested that being religious or spiritual boosts one's view of one's life, and having faith generally confers a greater benefit than turning to it as a means of coping. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chips smaller than rice grains wirelessly track heat during chemical reactions
item.description: A fleck-sized chip at the bottom of a test tube can provide researchers with data for every second of a chemical reaction while it is occurring. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why using a chatbot as your lawyer is a risky move—and ties up our court system
item.description: In the Federal Court of Australia, applications by self-represented litigants, many using artificial intelligence to research and draft their claims, have skyrocketed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Weight-loss drugs could reduce deaths and ease pressure on agricultural land by 2050
item.description: New research from the University of Aberdeen suggests weight-loss medications could deliver a double benefit, improving people's health while also helping the environment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cincinnati Zoo hopes a little shake will help Fiona the hippo pass a swallowed hat
item.description: The Cincinnati Zoo's animal care team has been working for days to help its beloved hippo Fiona safely digest and pass a knit cap she swallowed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Neutrons, death metal and a tiny prehistoric dragon: Scans reveal new horned reptile species from 156 million years ago
item.description: An unassuming fossil discovery in Wyoming caused quite a stir: Was it a baby dinosaur, a prehistoric snake or perhaps an entirely new species? Neutron imaging at the Paul Scherrer Institute PSI and the trained eye of a paleontologist eventually provided the answer: the 156-million-year-old fossil is that of a previously unknown species of reptile. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Diplomacy, humor and avoidance—what we found when we investigated friendships across class divides
item.description: Several years ago, the U.S. economist Raj Chetty and his team at Harvard University analyzed billions of ties on Facebook in a bid to learn more about social mobility. Their findings highlighted an important link between cross-class friendship and social mobility. Specifically, they found that people from low-income backgrounds who have more friends from wealthier backgrounds tend to have better chances of earning more as adults. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Newly discovered gut viruses offer clues to the origins of the smallpox virus family
item.description: Human and animal digestive systems host vast communities of microorganisms, including bacteria and viruses. Some are harmful, others are beneficial, and many remain poorly understood. In a recent study, scientists found an entirely new group of viruses without even having to go anywhere near anyone's innards. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Artificial wetland near Valencia traps 36% of incoming microplastics, study finds
item.description: The Tancat de la Pipa, an artificial wetland designed as a "green filter" for the Albufera de València, reduces microplastic pollution in the natural lagoon by 36%, according to research conducted by the Institute of Water and Environmental Engineering (IIAMA) at the Universitat Politècnica de València (UPV) and the Faculty of Environmental Sciences and Engineering at Babe–Bolyai University in Romania published in the journal Applied Sciences. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Black gobies are growing larger despite climate change
item.description: Researchers at the Department of Paleontology at the University of Vienna compared fossil and modern ear stones of the black goby (Gobius niger) from the northern Adriatic Sea to reconstruct its growth history over the past 8,000 years. The surprising result: while body size remained remarkably stable in the past, today's black gobies grow faster and reach larger sizes—even as the Adriatic Sea is warming rapidly. The study is now published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Science Data Powers New Method to Discover Hard-to-Find Pulsars
item.description: Open data from NASA’s Fermi mission helped an international team of scientists develop a method for finding pulsars about a million times faster than before. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: NASA Conducts Latest RS-25 Engine Test in Support of Future Artemis Missions
item.description: NASA tested RS-25 engine No. 10001 on Nov. 18 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi. Test teams fired the developmental engine for the planned duration of three minutes and 20 seconds (200 seconds). While this developmental engine will not be used in flight, the hot […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: LaToya Dean

item.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 Makes History Reaching One Light-Day From Earth
item.description: NASA’s Voyager 1 probe, humanity’s farthest-flying spacecraft, has reached one light-day from Earth, after more than 49 years of constant travel. A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, equaling about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers). The spacecraft achieved the milestone at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST) Nov. 18. Voyager team […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Taveau

item.title: Roaring back: Hong Kong’s 100-million-year-old dinosaur fossil makes its debut
item.description: Hong Kong’s first-ever dinosaur fossils, discovered on Port Island, belong to a sauropod measuring more than 20 metres (65 feet) long that lived about 100 million years ago, with the specimens going on public display on Friday. Traced to the Cretaceous period, the remains are among some 60 sets of rare dinosaur fossils on display at the Hong Kong Heritage Discovery Centre in Kowloon Park, including some from mainland China unveiled for the very first time in the city. “The discovery marks the... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Lexi Tian

item.title: Captan el primer saludo de Voyager 1 desde el otro lado de la frontera interestelar, a un día luz de distancia
item.description: Una antena de 70 metros de Madrid ha recibido este jueves una señal que la sonda de la NASA emitió 24 horas antes, a más de 25.902 millones de kilómetros de distancia Fuente: La Nación - El Mundo.

item.title: NASA's new Moon plans have a problem: Orion wasn't designed to fly this way
item.description: "We also have a responsibility to not go too fast and cut too many corners." Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: Eric Berger

item.title: Jeff Buckley was a 90s indie darling. Now gen Z think he’s the ‘yearner final boss’
item.description: With his unguarded lyricism and earnest delivery, the late singer-songwriter is having a moment among a generation that fetishizes unrequited desire Sydney Tripoli has collected Jeff Buckley memorabilia since 2019. She keeps her collection of T-shirts, posters, vinyl and other merch celebrating the late singer-songwriter in what she affectionately calls her “Buckley box”. The 27-year-old scours eBay and resale sites for these pieces; lately she’s noticed the prices “skyrocket”. “During the pandemic, it was impossible to find Jeff Buckley shirts. Now they’re everywhere on Depop,” said Tripoli… Fuente: The Guardian - Culture.
item.dc:creator: Alaina Demopoulos

item.title: AI maps overlooked housing to reveal gaps between Chicago's buildings and zoning rules
item.description: Duplexes, townhouses and small apartment buildings, often called mid-density housing, could help cities ease shortages and improve affordability. However, there is little data on how much of this housing exists. A new study by Yale School of the Environment scientists that focuses on Chicago found that it is widespread across the city, yet much of it sits in neighborhoods where current zoning doesn't allow that housing type. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Researchers use AI to optimize sensor design for ultrasensitive vitamin C detection
item.description: Researchers led by Professor Jinsung Park from the Department of Biomechatronic Engineering at Sungkyunkwan University (SKKU), have developed an ultrasensitive electrochemical sensor capable of detecting extremely low concentrations of vitamin C. By incorporating artificial intelligence (AI) into the sensor development process, the research team identified promising fabrication conditions using a limited amount of experimental data, reducing the need for extensive trial-and-error optimization. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Call to improve global ocean monitoring to prepare for marine heat waves
item.description: International experts are calling for marine heat waves to be tracked to inform strategies for sustaining fisheries and supporting communities reliant on oceans. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New genetic toolkit lets scientists engineer hard-to-study gut bacteria
item.description: One of the goals of gut microbiome research is that scientists will be able to develop treatments for various diseases that add or restore microbes with health benefits that are missing from the gut. This isn't as simple as just packing microbes into a probiotic capsule, though. Sometimes the most beneficial bacteria need a few tweaks before they can do their jobs. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Red crabs begin annual march to sea on Australia's Christmas Island
item.description: More than 100 million red crabs on Australia's Christmas Island have begun their annual migration from the forest to the sea, conservationists said this week. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins
item.description: A new study has uncovered a surprising concern hiding in popular plant-based foods and drinks. Researchers tested 212 vegan and vegetarian products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives, oat milk, almond milk, and soy milk, and found that every single one contained at least one potentially harmful fungal toxin. Known as mycotoxins, these naturally occurring compounds can contaminate grains, legumes, and seeds during farming and storage. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Study finds Islam on track to replace Christianity as biggest religion
item.description: The Pew Research Centre projects both groups will see their numbers increase over the next few decades, but the Muslim population will grow faster. Fuente: Africanews.

item.title: This 6-million-year-old whale may have had the most crooked face in mammal history
item.description: A bizarre whale that lived roughly 6 million years ago had a face so dramatically crooked that scientists believe it may have been the most asymmetrical of any mammal. Discovered in Peru, the extinct pygmy sperm whale Scaphokogia huachafo had an enormous downward-curving snout and a skull so distorted that researchers initially thought it had been damaged after death. Instead, its strange anatomy appears to have been an extraordinary evolutionary adaptation for hunting along the seafloor. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: X-rays tear water apart before its electrons can relax
item.description: A single X‑ray photon can break both O–H bonds in a water molecule within a few femtoseconds (quadrillionths of a second), creating neutral atomic oxygen. As shown by a study published in the journal Physical Review Letters, this breakup happens before the electrons finish relaxing, revealing an ultrafast pathway for X‑ray–driven chemistry in water. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs
item.description: Scientists have discovered a strange bacterium hiding beneath the skin of deep-sea creatures known as sea pigs, revealing an unexpected biological partnership. The microbe has an unusually tiny genome, yet more than a quarter of its DNA is devoted to making surface proteins, some of them exceptionally large. Researchers suspect it depends heavily on its host for survival, but what the sea pigs gain in return remains a mystery. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Cincinnati Zoo trying to shake loose Fiona the hippo after she swallowed a hat
item.description: Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo's famed hippo, underwent a colonoscopy this week, and now veterinarians are trying a new way to help her pass a knit cap that she swallowed after it slipped into her enclosure. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why hydrogen flames can glow orange, then turn nearly invisible
item.description: Hydrogen flames can shift from bright orange to nearly invisible depending on something unexpected: tiny amounts of sodium floating in the air. Scientists say this discovery could help make future hydrogen-powered stoves and ovens safer by replacing visual flame detection with specialized sensors. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Potatoes grown in simulated lunar soil match Earth-grown performance
item.description: Researchers have shown that potatoes grown in simulated lunar soil amended with organic matter are safe to eat and can achieve growth and yields comparable to those produced on Earth. "We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter," said Aymeric Goyer of Oregon State University's Department of Botany and Plant Pathology. "That's an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the moon." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist
item.description: A surprising new study suggests Antarctica's towering ice cliffs may be less vulnerable to catastrophic collapse than scientists once feared. After tracking more than 15,000 ice cliffs, researchers discovered that even the tallest cliffs, which can collapse at alarming speeds, often stabilize rather than triggering an unstoppable chain reaction. Underwater ridges, surrounding water, and broken ice appear to provide natural defenses against further collapse. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Why don't weight-loss drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy work for everyone?
item.description: Why do Ozempic and Wegovy produce dramatic weight loss for some people but disappointing results for others? Scientists are investigating whether the body's hidden energy-saving response could help explain the difference and unlock more effective, personalized weight-loss treatments. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: En la COP31, los ministros intentan desbloquear las negociaciones para adoptar un texto final
item.description: Los ministros reunidos en la COP31 en Antalya, Turquía, intentaron desbloquear las negociaciones el miércoles 18 de noviembre por la noche, ante las diferencias sobre el abandono de los combustibles fósiles, el financiamiento climático y la ciencia. Se espera un nuevo borrador del texto final para acercar posiciones antes del viernes, plazo previsto para alcanzar un acuerdo. Fuente: France 24 - Español.

item.title: El Niño Rains Paint the Atacama
item.description: Winter precipitation helped wake dormant seeds in northern Chile, carpeting the desert with what may be the region’s most extensive flowering of the satellite era. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Expert comment: UK roads are dangerous by design. Punishing bad drivers won't fix them
item.description: In 2025, 1.16 million people around the world were killed in road collisions. That's 3,178 deaths per day. Up to 50 million were injured. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The art of success: Study shows arts education benefits students with disabilities
item.description: Give students with disabilities greater access to the arts, and good things happen: They come to school more often, face fewer disciplinary problems and improve their writing skills, according to new research from the University of Missouri. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Stonehenge’s six-ton mystery deepens as scientists narrow their search
item.description: A major new investigation into Stonehenge’s mysterious six-ton Altar Stone has uncovered fresh clues while ruling out several suspected sources. Once thought to have originated in Wales, the massive sandstone slab is now believed to have come from northeastern Scotland, although researchers have yet to find an exact match. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Exquisite X-rays and dynamic compression initiate a new era of physics experiments on plutonium
item.description: Scientists at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL), Argonne National Laboratory (ANL) and Washington State University (WSU) have conducted the first dynamic compression experiments on plutonium at a national light source facility, the Dynamic Compression Sector (DCS). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden hereditary form of aggressive prostate cancer
item.description: Scientists have discovered a rare inherited mutation in the CDK12 gene linked to aggressive prostate cancer, with all five identified carriers developing metastatic disease between ages 44 and 62. The finding could lead to expanded genetic testing, helping families uncover hidden cancer risks and potentially detect the disease while it is still treatable. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Policy changes in Canada had little effect on sales of antibiotics for animals, study finds
item.description: Sales of antibiotics for use in food-producing animals have fallen by 11% in Canada since 2018, but not because of federal policy changes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ancient minerals reveal a missing chapter in Türkiye's mountain-building history
item.description: A mountain range can bear the marks of events from tens of millions of years ago. The challenge lies in determining when each mark was created. In southern Türkiye's Central Taurides, scientists have developed a method to date some of these ancient movements by examining tiny calcite deposits that formed as faults shifted. This new timeline alters the region's geological history. Researchers discovered a previously unrecognized period during which parts of the crust slid laterally, between the Early Eocene and Early Miocene. They also found that the region's later extension began around 25… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New mixing benchmark could help industry reduce energy use in stirred tanks
item.description: Solid–liquid mixing, where particles are dispersed in a liquid, is essential in many industrial processes such as slurry preparation, crystallization, precipitation, adsorption and dissolution. In such cases, effective mixing is critical for contact between particles and liquid, enabling mass transfer. Floating particles often pose a challenge in mixing because they are lighter than the liquid and tend to float at its surface. While impeller agitation does draw them into the liquid, the minimum mixing intensity needed for effective drawdown has been difficult to define. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Is free will an illusion? New brain research reveals a surprising twist
item.description: New research reveals that the brain makes free choices and forced decisions using surprisingly similar neural processes, with activity building toward a decision before we act. The discovery challenges assumptions about free will while suggesting that our personal preferences and experiences still shape what we choose. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Researchers trace how gut microbes transform dietary plant sterols into circulating sulfated metabolites
item.description: Phytosterols are plant-derived compounds found in vegetable oils, nuts and seeds. They are studied for their ability to reduce cholesterol absorption, yet only about 5% enter the circulation and most are excreted. How gut bacteria influence their metabolism and tissue distribution has remained unclear. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: US-China science ties fray as visa hurdles and security scrutiny grow
item.description: Peking University professor Li Yulong’s team celebrated when six scientists detailing their research on detecting neural signals were accepted for the Society for Neuroscience’s 56th annual meeting in Washington – but only four obtained US visas to participate in it. Li has been regularly attending the world’s largest neuroscience gathering since he was a student in 2000. He described it as an essential forum for sharing findings with researchers worldwide, but said his team’s visa difficulties... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: Should we save every old building?
item.description: When you visit one of Norway's open-air museums, you can experience a piece of old Norway: log-built timber houses, farmsteads and farm complexes, often situated in a historic cultural landscape. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: First lunar-specific ground motion model could guide seismic hazard assessments on moon
item.description: Civil engineers looking forward to building structures on the moon need to know how ground motion from moonquakes will affect these buildings. But will ground motion models developed for Earth work well for the lunar landscape? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Watch: Sea level rise isn't just waves—how groundwater threatens coastal cities from below
item.description: With El Niño winter storms rolling in, coastal communities will naturally brace for the obvious: surging high tides, pounding waves and seawater spilling over seawalls. Decades of storm coverage have encouraged us to measure climate risk by what crashes onto the shoreline. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The philosophical reason AI Christmas ads leave audiences feeling cold
item.description: It's that time of year when Christmas ads start appearing, and brands offer up a slice of consumerist comfort as you curl up in front of a screen. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A 115 million‑year‑old 'algae rebellion' in Portugal's sea cliffs pushes back evolutionary timeline
item.description: Quite a few scientific discoveries are a product of chance. You set out looking for one thing, but often end up finding something totally unexpected. In micropaleontology, the study of microscopic fossils, this is especially common. You never know what you're going to find until you start examining the samples under the microscope. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Atoms in sync: Superradiance offers a new kind of frequency comb
item.description: When scientists shine a laser beam into a crystal, they typically expect a steady glow as the crystal's atoms are energized and begin to emit light. But in early 2024, while searching for something else entirely, researchers in the lab of Caltech's Andrei Faraon saw a crystal flash in a regular rhythm, like a metronome keeping a beat. The flashes came from billions of atoms embedded in the crystal. Coupled to a tiny superconducting circuit, the atoms had become synchronized and started emitting light together through a special quantum phenomenon known as superradiance. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Q&A: Schools that ban cellphones see uptick in test scores
item.description: We're nearing two milestones in the smartphone era. January will mark 20 years since Steve Jobs first unveiled the iPhone from a stage in San Francisco. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Reading the temperature fingerprints of electrocatalytic reactions
item.description: Electrocatalysis is key to turning renewable electricity into fuels and chemicals, and industrial electrolyzers typically operate at moderately elevated temperatures. Measuring how reaction rates change with temperature is also a powerful, yet underexplored, way to probe what controls them. Such measurements yield two quantities: an apparent activation enthalpy, reflecting the energetic cost of the reaction, and a prefactor, which is linked to the activation entropy. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Even AI thinks it's a man's job: Models reveal gender bias in resumes and hiring assessments
item.description: The first hurdle may arise even before an application is submitted. A woman asks artificial intelligence to help her write her resume: The system chooses words, highlights qualities and builds a profile. Then another system, perhaps based on the same model, evaluates that text. If both reproduce gender stereotypes, the risk is a double filter: Bias enters the application and is reinforced by the person selecting it. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 hits record one light-day distance, 50 years after launch
item.description: Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth, marking a historic milestone nearly 50 years after its 1977 launch. Fuente: Al Jazeera English.
